idiom_name: Enumerable#each with a block (internal iteration) + Enumerator/Enumerator::Lazy for external iteration
implementation_notes: Ruby has no Iterator class and needs none: the canonical realization is internal iteration - the aggregate includes Enumerable, defines one each method that yields every element to a block, and all other traversals (map/select/find/reduce/take_while) are derived from that single primitive, so the representation stays hidden and the client passes behaviour into the collection instead of pulling values out. For external iteration - pulling one value at a time, two cursors over one collection, lazy chains - Enumerator is the bridge: obj.to_enum/obj.enum_for(:each) wraps any each-based method as an object with next/peek (raising StopIteration at the end, implemented with a Fiber), and Enumerable#lazy returns an Enumerator::Lazy whose map/select/take_while chain without evaluating until a non-lazy method forces it. Hand-write a cursor object only when the traversal genuinely cannot be expressed as each over a source.
code_sketch:
class Inventory
  include Enumerable
  def initialize(items) = @items = items
  def each(&block)                     # single primitive; the rest is derived
    @items.each(&block)                # representation @items stays hidden
  end
end
inventory.select(&:pending?).map(&:amount)   # internal iteration, block-driven
cursor = inventory.each                      # Enumerator: .next / .peek
inventory.lazy.select(&:pending?).first(3)   # lazy chain, forced by .first
pitfalls: Blocks are not objects and each returns the receiver, so a method that forgets to yield its block silently returns an Enumerator instead of raising - callers then get an empty traversal.

External iteration through Enumerator#next runs the source in a Fiber: it is substantially slower than internal each, and mixing next/peek with block-form methods on the same Enumerator advances the cursor out of sync.
Enumerator::Lazy defers everything until a forcing call: an unmaterialised chain runs zero work, and a lazy chain over an infinite source must be truncated (first/take) or the program hangs.
Enumerable methods materialise (to_a/map/sort) before returning, so chains over huge collections need lazy or an explicit each-with-accumulator instead.
